full_text:
**Verdict: KNOWN-VARIANT, medium confidence.** The pattern sequence is well documented for nonlocal-competition birth–death and logistic models. I found no source that uses a three-body death term as the control parameter, or that reports the spot–stripe–spot re-entry in this particle system.

**1. Model family**

This is a spatial birth–death point process with Gaussian dispersal and a nonlocal competition kernel. It is the Bolker–Pacala–Dieckmann–Law (BPDL) class. A long-range competition radius (1.25) much larger than the dispersal width (0.05) gives a finite-wavelength, Turing-like instability. The pair-plus-three-body death rate adds a higher-order nonlinearity to the usual nonlocal logistic or Fisher–KPP model.

**2. What the literature shows**

- **Model class.** The BPDL process was introduced by Bolker and Pacala and by Dieckmann and Law. This model was introduced by Bolker and Pacala [2] and Dieckmann and Law [9]. The Bolker and Pacala moment-equation papers cover endogenous spatial structure. The moment equations predict endogenous spatial pattern formation.
- **Earliest particle-based source I found.** Hernández-García and López (2004, Phys. Rev. E 70, 016216) studied a birth–death particle model with neighbourhood-dependent rates. The model shows an inhomogeneous quasistationary pattern with many different clusters of particles arranged periodically in space. They derived a macroscopic density equation and show that there is a finite-wavelength instability leading to pattern formation.
- **Earlier continuum precursor.** Britton's nonlocal competition models are the roots of this line of work. A later paper says the research on the nonlocal model can be traced back to Britton [5, 6]. I did not open Britton's papers, so I can't give his exact title or year.
- **Competition-only patterns.** Martínez-García, Calabrese, Hernández-García and López (2013, Geophys. Res. Lett.) showed that competition alone gives the full pattern set. We recover the full spectrum of spatial structures typical of vegetation models that also account for facilitation in addition to competition. That spectrum is gaps, stripes and spots. They also describe one mechanism in which competition enters through the death rate.
- **Review.** Martínez-García et al. (2014, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A 372, 20140068) reviewed models in which finite-range competition is the only driving force.
- **Hexagonal spots, stripes and gaps as one sequence.** Nonlinear analyses of the vegetation logistic equations report hexagonal spot, stripe and hexagonal gap patterns. A hexagonal spotted pattern formed, changing into labyrinths for R=1; while a hexagonal gap pattern was generated for R=1.25. The same source notes stripes and spots (or stripes and gaps) are predicted, the initial conditions determine which stable equilibrium pattern of each pair will be selected. A cellular-automaton study also reports a shift from spots through labyrinths to gaps under competition only. A flow paper on the nonlocal FKPP equation reports gap, labyrinth/stripe and hexagonal-spot regimes.
- **Why a nonlinearity parameter and re-entry are plausible.** Generic pattern-selection theory says quadratic terms favour spots or hexagons and cubic terms favour stripes. A pattern-formation text states if cubic terms dominate, then rolls (or stripes) prevail. Murray's book says the same. Spots, then stripes, then spots again as the nonlinearity or ratio is tuned fits this picture. Spots, stripes and inverted spots appear in classical 2D Turing systems too (Stripes, spots, or reversed spots in two-dimensional Turing systems, J. Theor. Biol.; I did not confirm the authors or year).

**3. What differs and whether it matters**

- I found no paper that uses a three-body (density-squared, short-range) death term as the tuned parameter in a continuous-space particle model.
- I also found no paper reporting spot–stripe–spot re-entry as the death/birth ratio is varied in such a model.
- The generic mechanism (long-range competition plus a tunable nonlinearity) should carry over. Weakly nonlinear theory would likely explain the stripe window and the re-entry. The exact thresholds (g values, ratio 0.55) are specific to these parameters and are not in the literature.
- The anisotropy index jumping from 0 to 1 at stripe onset is probably a descriptor choice, not a new effect.

**4. Confidence and limits**

Confidence is medium. The model family and the spots/stripes/gaps sequence are well supported, but I read only abstracts and snippets, not full texts. My search budget was limited, so the specific three-body and re-entry claims may exist in sources I did not reach. The citation details below were checked against the search results, except Britton's papers and the reversed-spots paper.
